For the past half an hour, I've tried to write a note describing my very special relationship with museums, but I seem to be unable to transcribe the emotions I feel when I think of the different moments spent there. items.title: Watching travel advice maps change
items.label: Small Web
items.excerpt:
I have always been impressed by the Australian government’s Smartraveller updates. In particular, I find its maps surprisingly detailed. For a while I had thought it would be neat to save those maps and play them back later as a small timelapse.

So I started downloading them and storing them in an SQLite database. Once I had added a scraper for Australia, it seemed natural to add the equivalent Danish and UK departments too. Then I kept going.

Travel Advice now archives advice hourly from Australia, Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, New Zealand, Spain, Sweden, the UK and the US. It lets you compare their current advice and follow the changes as they happen.

The first map change I caught was France updating its advice for Guatemala:

items.title: In the fog of AI
items.label: Blogs
items.excerpt:
The other day I couldn’t see far because of heavy fog, and as I pedalled across the Erasmus Bridge I wondered: isn’t this fog a perfect metaphor for not knowing where we are in this age of AI?

There was a national weather alert, but that didn’t stop me from getting on my bike as usual. If anything, I expected the motorways to be a mess on a day like this.

When we can’t see clearly ahead, the natural response is to slow down in order to prevent accidents. And while most of us do, it has little effect when others carry on at their normal pace.

Where on a Bulgarian motorway a major traffic accident happened because of the fog, we see software security incidents happen more frequently than ever before: vulnerabilities are found and exploited faster than they can be mitigated (like PHP2Shell ). There’s no slowing down.

It was cold and my jacket was all wet because of the water particles surrounding me. When I neared the bridge, the fog seemed to intensify. On the bridge I could barely…

I do the dishes almost every day. Each time, I'm confronted by the sponge that I use to scrub my pots, pans, and tea-stained drinkwares. Like most sponge normies, I started off with your classic squishy-bottom-sponge-with-a-scrubber on top combo:

Once you use these long enough, you notice how they break down over time. Green flecks start flaking off the top, and chunks of both the top and bottom layers eventually tear off. They might get caught in your cookware. They definitely end up down the drain and into the sewer system, and probably into a beautiful lake or river somewhere.

Not to mention all the invisible microplastics. It's gross!

Right, let's buy some sponges made of natural materials.

I tried some 'natural' brands with a cellulose-sponge base and a walnut scrubber top, but for some reason those also contained plastic. Maybe in the scrubber? They were also pricier.

items.label: Hobbies and Creative
items.excerpt:
Georgia O'Keeffe, “Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I,” 1930. (Photo: Christie’s Images Ltd.)

You never know what could be hiding in someone’s closet. Earlier this year, a long-lost Georgia O’Keeffe painting was discovered in the closet of a woman’s Manhattan apartment, and was recently presented as part of Christie’s 20th Century Evening Sale in New York.

The 1930 painting, Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I, was estimated to be worth between $3 million and $5 million. On Nov. 17, it sold at auction for $4.8 million. It depicts the tan, green, and brown rolling mountains of New Mexico, using O’Keeffe’s signature sweeping curves that bring the viewer’s eye across the landscape. O’Keeffe first visited New Mexico in 1929 and it would continue to inspire her to paint throughout her career.

items.title: 💬 Snippet!
items.label: Small Web
items.excerpt:
What happens when words disappear, when they escape and run away? 

When I write of darkness; a wish to share, to tell you —you are not alone, I was there too.  

Yet the words shout —No! —and off they go, packed up their bags, dragged them over the floor; for it was heavy, heavy baggage of my heart, off they go. 

Where do they go, that rebellious testimony of my humanity, witness of suffering, flickering of the light? Where do they hide? It seems the ink had not dried.

Why do some words run away and others stay? 

I guess I should be grateful, for he will never gaze at the darkness of that dream. 

#100words_100days #poetry #words

items.title: Getting over daddy issues: abandonment edition
items.label: Q&A
items.excerpt:
I'm looking for resources or advice to get over abandonment issues, specifically from a biological father who was never there.

My biological dad has never been in my life. I have a few fleeting early-childhood memories of him coming over to my house, having sex with my mom, completely ignoring me, and leaving. Other than that I have never seen or met this man.

When I was around 5-6 my mom married my step-dad, who for all intents and purposes I consider to be my dad. Then he died when I was in my mid-20s. I'm resentful that the guy who chose to raise me got cancer and died, while the guy who never wanted to be in my life is still alive and well.

items.title: Feed the Scorchpot [$14.99] [Strategy] [Windows] [macOS]
items.label: Gaming
items.excerpt:
You struck a deal with a dragon: twenty years of protection for twenty years of dinner service. The island thrives under the beast's watchful eye, as long as the meals keep coming.

Every year, the dragon wakes up hungrier. You roll dice to work your island, harvest ingredients, fuse them into recipes, and cook them down in the Scorchpot — the pot you keep full or end up in. Get the meal right and you prosper. Get it wrong and you're smoke.

Build farmsteads, shrines, and harbors across your hex-grid island, each one changing how the board pays out. The best runs start with a handful of tiles and end with a machine that buries the dragon in food. Then the odds tighten, the dragon turns picky, and you tear the whole thing down and rebuild while it's on fire.

Feed the Scorchpot, keep the dragon happy, and outlast the contract.
